c67198208cd6.en: Ad platforms report an order the moment a customer checks out. In Pakistani cash-on-delivery, that's the start of the funnel, not the end. Nearly a third of orders were cancelled on the confirmation call before a parcel ever moved, and another fifth came back as returns.

4ed9db71dbd4.en: Confirmation-calling every order before dispatch caught roughly 325 of the bad ones early, saving an estimated <t0>PKR 78,650</t0> in courier fees that would otherwise have gone out and come straight back.

df1211f3c98e.en: Snapchat bought attention 4–6x cheaper than Meta. TikTok bought nothing.

ebd1b1651580.en: Meta ran roughly <t0>PKR 15,000</t0> of budget on campaigns that never produced a sale, left on because nobody was checking below the account-level number. TikTok spent PKR 6,412 and produced about five orders, all cancelled at confirmation.

a2f95ea6620d.en: The highest-priced product also had the best delivery rate.

320f97b543df.en: Order value vs. delivery rate, by product

ba41fe4c7a9e.en: The pattern ran opposite to what we expected going in, the cheapest item did not deliver the best. A buyer paying more per order seems to think it through more before ordering, and follows through more often when the rider arrives.

bd8704518e16.en: Stock buying didn't reflect this at the time: the best-performing product was reordered the least, and the weakest was reordered the most. That's the gap the next round of buying is built to close.

8f67ee2b7ee6.en: <t0>Delivery, By City Not Just By Courier</t0>

f99b5a9c169a.en: The worst-performing courier just happened to ship the most parcels to the worst-performing city.

ce56b466137f.en: Read on its own, one courier looked far weaker than the others. Split by destination, every courier underperformed in the same city, the courier gap was mostly geography wearing a different name.

a19ba4039567.en: Delivery success by city · top markets by volume

0b5bfd0e7f0a.en: Eight months of testing across three ad platforms, three shipped products and two couriers produced a working funnel model, a channel comparison worth acting on, and a clear read on which products and which cities were actually worth scaling.

b1bc4bb2020c.en: The media buying was genuinely excellent: <t0>11 million impressions for PKR 471,193</t0>, a click-through rate of 2.19%, and video ads that held attention through nearly 40% of a 2-second view.

0302f2a11091.en: Confirmation-calling every order before dispatch is a habit that transfers to any store, it saved roughly <t0>PKR 78,650</t0> in courier costs that would otherwise have been spent and refunded.

d3337ad4c8a0.en: We switched from dropshipping to owned stock mid-flight once it was clear dropshipping was capping how much of the operation we could actually control, the kind of call that's easy to avoid making and costly to delay.

abb93cdb07cc.en: Eight product types were tested across the run, not one, which is how the best-performing product got found at all.

fd6794f42eb6.en: Never sell a product that's price-anchored on Daraz or Temu, if a customer can price-check it against ten identical listings in ten seconds, you're competing on price before the ad even runs.

2fa91ae9cf72.en: Judge a product on how it performs through the whole funnel, order value and delivery rate together, not on how good it looks on the product page.

0f020a099fd1.en: Track delivery rate by city from day one, not just by courier, a 26-point gap between two cities went unnoticed for months because nobody split the data that way.

208f00f0473c.en: Offer a prepaid discount from week one, prepaid orders return at roughly a quarter of cash-on-delivery's rate.

399e31cd3b1b.en: Buy stock in proportion to what's already proven to sell. AlphaMart's best product got the least stock and its worst product got the most.

a0ee30c96251.en: When a month works, put more into it, the best month of the business was followed by a 76% cut in ad spend, for reasons that had nothing to do with performance.

dccd63af92c2.en: <t0>Google → Google: 96% inbox.</t0> Content, SPF, DKIM and DMARC all passed. Spam-filter score 0, no blacklists.

6d37d3447e62.en: <t0>Google → Microsoft: 0% inbox, 100% spam.</t0> Every email to an Outlook or Microsoft 365 address was landing in junk.

95cd3a3300ab.en: That isolated the failure to <t0>sender reputation with Microsoft</t0>. Content, authentication and blacklisting were all ruled out. For a B2B audience, where a large share of companies run on Microsoft 365, that alone explains most of the missing replies.

8852683d97dc.en: The fix plan: register with Microsoft SNDS/JMRP, add 2–3 sending domains on a second provider, cap volume at 25–40 emails per mailbox per day, segment sends by the recipient's mail provider, and turn off open tracking. eb4d27fb1768.en: Duplicate Purchase Events After Adding the Conversions API

0f6af116cfb9.en: The Meta pixel and Conversions API should deduplicate to one event. When they do not, you double-count revenue or lose half of it. How to prove yours works.

6ea31f6eeeec.en: Running the Meta pixel and Conversions API together should deduplicate to one event. When it does not, you either double-count revenue or silently lose half of it. How deduplication actually works and how to prove yours is functioning.

b6488b214742.en: Why am I seeing duplicate purchase events after installing the Conversions API?

d02851a3f3fd.en: Because the browser pixel and the server are both sending the purchase, and Meta cannot tell they are the same event. Deduplication requires both sides to send a matching event_id, and ideally the same event_name. If the IDs differ, Meta counts two separate purchases.

3e965e036b0e.en: What is event_id used for in the Meta Conversions API?

9052746ac867.en: It is the deduplication key. When the pixel and the Conversions API both send an event with the same event_name and the same event_id within Meta deduplication window, Meta keeps one and discards the other.

10834c347d50.en: Is it bad to run the Meta pixel and Conversions API at the same time?

a0abf0b93561.en: No, running both is the recommended setup because the server side captures conversions the browser misses. It is only a problem when deduplication is misconfigured, in which case you either double-count or lose events.

359a65da0b3f.en: You installed CAPI and your revenue doubled. It didn’t.

0b7dbfe8f737.en: Duplicate purchases after a Conversions API install almost always mean one thing: <t0>the browser and the server are sending different <t1>event_id</t1> values</t0> for the same purchase. Meta deduplicates on matching <t2>event_name</t2> plus <t3>event_id</t3>. If the IDs differ, it has no way to know the two events are the same order, so it counts both.

7161a8c9a23b.en: The dangerous version is the opposite failure, where IDs collide and you silently lose real sales.

58e3629d1967.en: Installing the Conversions API is the right decision. Browser tracking loses events to ad blockers, tracking prevention, broken sessions and abandoned page loads, and a server-side feed recovers a good share of them. Almost everyone should be running both.

07c25361904b.en: But “running both” means Meta now receives two reports of every purchase, and the only thing stopping it counting each one twice is a shared identifier. Get that identifier wrong in one direction and your revenue doubles on paper. Get it wrong in the other and your revenue quietly halves.

ac4da9970dda.en: Meta matches on two fields together: <t0>event_name</t0> and <t1>event_id</t1>. Both must agree.

a24d080805d8.en: The rule is simple to state and easy to break in practice, because the two sides are usually built by different systems at different times. The browser event is generated by a theme or a tag manager; the server event is generated by an app, a middleware service, or your own code. Nothing forces them to agree, and nothing warns you when they do not.

68b8be996d72.en: Choosing an identifier that cannot drift

75460a7f9f74.en: The identifier must be <t0>unique per order</t0> and <t1>identical across both paths</t1>. Those two requirements rule out most of what people reach for first.

cad331f39cfd.en: Yes, if both read the order

1981bf2a493e.en: Only if generated once and passed

58bb7dcc26b4.en: Timestamps are the worst offender and the most tempting, because they look unique. They are not: two orders in the same second collide, and the browser’s clock is not your server’s clock. A UUID is fine <t0>only</t0> if it is generated once and then passed to the other side, if each side generates its own, you have built a duplication machine.

dcca98b90eb7.en: Everyone worries about double-counting because it is visible. The worse bug is an identifier that is not unique, a checkout ID reused across orders, or a value that repeats. Then Meta correctly deduplicates two <t0>genuinely different</t0> purchases into one, and you lose real revenue from your reporting with no error anywhere.

72001fe8856c.en: Double-counting looks like good news and gets investigated. Silent loss looks like a slow decline and gets blamed on the ads.

550a5d5689e0.en: Proving it works: not assuming it does

3505d040a316.en: Configured is not the same as working. Here is the test that settles it, and it takes about fifteen minutes.

f145d2def990.en: <t0>Place one real order</t0>A real purchase through the real checkout, not a test link. Note the order number.

09c473ee8659.en: <t0>Capture the browser event ID</t0>Open DevTools before checking out, filter the Network tab for <t1>facebook</t1>, complete the order, and read the <t2>eventID</t2> on the Purchase request.

dcc17971139d.en: <t0>Capture the server event ID</t0>From your CAPI integration’s logs, or from Events Manager, find the server-side event for that same order and read its <t1>event_id</t1>.

ae6ab29d529a.en: <t0>Compare them character for character</t0>Not similar. Identical. A prefix on one side (<t1>order_1047</t1> versus <t2>1047</t2>) is a failure, not a detail.

6ae9cc0c04d5.en: <t0>Check the deduplication reporting</t0>In Events Manager, open the Purchase event and look at how it is being received. A correctly deduplicated setup shows both browser and server as sources for the same event, not two separate event totals.

54e99d24b32a.en: <t0>Reconcile a full week</t0>Compare your store’s order count with Events Manager purchases for a settled week. Meaningfully above your order count means duplication. Meaningfully below means loss.

62183144136b.en: The number that tells you it is working

7c1cae747321.en: Once deduplication is right, the metric worth watching is <t0>Event Match Quality</t0>. It reflects how much identifying information you send with each event, hashed email, phone, name, location, click identifiers, and it drives how well Meta can attribute a conversion to the person who saw the ad.

debc662381be.en: This is where the Conversions API earns its keep. Your server knows the customer’s email and phone number because they just bought something. The browser often does not. Sending that data server-side, correctly hashed, is usually a bigger win than recovering the blocked events in the first place.

675a8e43cb4a.en: <t0>Hash it, and check that you did</t0>

1d463b2143b2.en: Customer identifiers must be SHA-256 hashed before they are sent. This is not a performance nicety, it is the difference between sending Meta a hash and sending Meta your customers’ raw personal data. If you are building the integration yourself, verify the hashing on a real payload before you go live, because a bug here is a data protection incident rather than a tracking bug.

f906da2640f3.en: I have not given you a target Event Match Quality score or an expected uplift from installing CAPI. Both depend entirely on what customer data you can legitimately collect, your checkout, and your traffic, and every benchmark I have seen published comes from a vendor whose product improves the number they are benchmarking.

55b7f711e115.en: Measure your own baseline before the change, measure again after it has run for a full attribution window, and compare against yourself. That comparison is worth more than anyone’s published average.

40184cda3be7.en: Not sure if your deduplication is working?

3b3d85b73b44.en: It is a fifteen-minute check and most setups fail it. Send me your store URL and I will tell you what I find.

8ad5b37eb608.en: A Google Ads account audit for lead generation: six checks, in order

0d09a2a26b35.en: A useful Google Ads audit for a business that lives on phone calls and enquiry forms checks six things in order: advertiser verification, Search and Display separation, location targeting, negative keywords, conversion tracking for forms and calls, and ad group structure by service.

5f730cbafc91.en: I ran this sequence on a dental clinic's account that had never been properly configured.

6782b1b442e0.en: Most Google Ads audit checklists start with bids and ad copy. For a lead-generation business I start further upstream, because bids and copy cannot repair an account that shows ads in the wrong place, to the wrong searches, with no record of what happened next.

b797ebeb0610.en: Google can require advertiser identity verification. On the clinic's account it had not been completed, which put campaign delivery at risk. Look for a verification notice first, because nothing else matters if ads stop serving.

84ea06a1e4eb.en: The clinic's campaigns mixed the Search and Display Networks. Display was using budget without producing enquiries, so I separated the two and paused Display. Check the network settings of every campaign.

8885e792b40f.en: The campaigns targeted the whole world instead of Islamabad, where the clinic operates. Open each campaign's location settings and confirm the places listed are the places you serve.

5d09a1b11f38.en: There were no negative keywords, so a share of the budget went to searches with no local intent. Read the search terms report for the last 30 days and add what should never have triggered an ad.

8070e6e94102.en: Conversion tracking for forms and calls

06df19125f75.en: Neither form submissions nor phone calls were tracked, so every decision rested on clicks alone. I set up Google Tag Manager triggers for form submissions and click-to-call taps and linked those events to Google Ads.

0823b041e4d9.en: I researched local search terms and grouped keywords by service, such as teeth cleaning, implants and whitening, so each ad can match what the person typed.

66ae284eedaa.en: What changed on the clinic's account

1d947d48f7ab.en: After the rebuild the account was Search-only, targeted to Islamabad, with a negative keyword list and tracking in place. For the first time the clinic could see which ads, keywords and campaigns produced real patient enquiries.

860c41e0ca82.en: Google Ads Call Tracking for Local Service Businesses

3d47adda8edc.en: Most tracking guides assume an online store. If your conversion is a phone call, the failures differ. Four ways to track Google Ads calls, and where each fails.

f7bee19c9081.en: Almost every conversion tracking guide is written for online stores. If your conversion is a phone call, the failure modes are completely different. Here are the four ways to track calls from Google Ads, what each one actually measures, and where they go wrong.

0030c9a24d4a.en: How do I track phone calls from Google Ads?

0e56b8a1370d.en: There are four methods: call extensions using a Google forwarding number, calls from a website using a dynamic number swap, static click-to-call tracking, and a third-party call tracking platform. Each measures something slightly different, and only some of them attribute the call back to a specific keyword.

2b22a65cea2b.en: Does Google Ads call tracking record calls?

e6900e4e22a0.en: Google Ads can record calls made through Google forwarding numbers where the feature is available, and this is subject to local law and disclosure requirements. Tracking that a call happened and recording its contents are separate decisions with separate legal obligations.

9db6a1e66133.en: Why does Google Ads show calls but my phone did not ring?

1fe2810d6ab5.en: A common cause is counting click-to-call taps as calls. A tap on a phone link is an intent to call, not a completed call. If you track taps rather than connected calls of a minimum duration, your reported conversions will exceed the calls you actually received.

d1549a62e3df.en: Google Ads call tracking, for businesses whose customers ring instead of buy

48597bea8bd6.en: If your conversion is a phone call rather than a checkout, almost every tracking guide online is written for someone else. There are four ways to track calls from Google Ads: <t0>call extensions, dynamic number insertion on your website, static click-to-call, and a third-party platform</t0>, and they measure different things.

4787446104dd.en: The most common mistake is counting a tap on a phone link as a call. It is not one. It is an intention.

be74ac964053.en: Read any article about conversion tracking and you will find yourself in an ecommerce store. Purchase events, cart values, return on ad spend. That is not much use if you are a dentist, a carpet cleaner, a plumber or a physiotherapist, where the money arrives because someone picked up a phone.

ef4eb78601aa.en: The failure modes are genuinely different, and they are worse, because a phone call leaves no trace in your website analytics at all unless you deliberately make it leave one.

23b9c2027f29.en: The four methods, and what each one really tells you

d871c99b262e.en: Calls placed directly from the ad

01a0a10b309b.en: Misses everyone who clicks through to the site first

bbffdb9a7813.en: Calls to a swapped number on your site

9669bde9fd6d.en: Needs the swap script to load and work on mobile

0c783c956f7d.en: Counts intent, not connection, inflates conversions

b8ccbb777715.en: Monthly cost; another system to maintain

f70447db666a.en: Notice the third row. It is the one most small businesses end up with, usually by accident, because tracking a tap is the easiest thing to set up in Google Tag Manager. It is also the one that lies to you the most.

0cdea2435c54.en: Why counting taps quietly destroys your bidding

916984913936.en: A tap on a <t0>tel:</t0> link means someone was interested enough to open their dialler. It does not mean they pressed the green button. It does not mean you answered. It does not mean the call lasted longer than four seconds before they realised you were closed.

1a6f175a2f37.en: If you feed taps into Google Ads as conversions, Smart Bidding optimises toward <t0>people who tap</t0>. Those are not the same people as <t1>customers who book</t1>. The gap between the two is where your budget goes.

c31514a54044.en: The single highest-leverage change most local advertisers can make is applying a <t0>minimum call duration</t0> before a call counts as a conversion. Sixty seconds is a sensible starting point for most service businesses: long enough to exclude wrong numbers and immediate hang-ups, short enough to include a quick “can you come Tuesday?”

f80af713ddc3.en: What I actually set up, and what it changed

fa9816860d65.en: I have built this twice, for two very different businesses, and it is the part of my work with the clearest before-and-after.

cfdce4a2516f.en: Google Ads + GTM · call and form tracking

04f4a5fe4a53.en: Before: Google Ads was running with no view of which searches produced appointments. Enquiries arrived by phone and by form, and neither was attributed to anything.

23e2335192a6.en: After: GTM tracking on both enquiry forms and phone calls, so specific searches could be tied to actual appointments for the first time. In the clinic’s words, they “stopped guessing.”

41d60e968d0a.en: <t0>What I am not claiming:</t0> I do not have a published cost-per-enquiry figure for this account, so I am not going to invent one. What changed was visibility, which is the prerequisite for everything else, not the outcome itself.

5911ac4e45dd.en: The second was <t0>Mr Expert Carpet Cleaning</t0> in Slough, where the site was rebuilt from scratch with tracking designed in rather than bolted on, including a server-side GTM container. That one taught me the lesson in the next section.

e73687eafd92.en: The failure nobody warns you about: the form that emails

83a249480f0b.en: Most local service sites use a contact form that composes an email and sends it. If that send fails, a bad SMTP configuration, a spam filter, a full inbox, the lead does not go to a queue for retry. It ceases to exist. There is no record that anyone ever filled the form in.

96c59ad4de18.en: You cannot track what was never saved. So before any conversion tracking work on a local service site, I check one thing: <t0>does the form write the lead to a database before it tries to email anyone?</t0> If the answer is no, tracking is the second problem.

e77fdff46237.en: This is the order that matters. Write the lead to storage, then attempt the email, the CRM push, the WhatsApp alert and the conversion event. Every one of those can fail without losing the enquiry. Reverse the order and a single failure loses a customer silently.

ce55143ca67a.en: <t0>Make the lead durable first</t0>Ensure form submissions are stored somewhere that is not an inbox. Everything downstream is optional; this is not.

20540d6551f7.en: <t0>Turn on call assets with a forwarding number</t0>This captures the people who ring straight from the ad without ever visiting your site, usually a bigger share than owners expect.

cb64eb12842a.en: <t0>Add website call tracking with number swapping</t0>So calls made after landing on the site are attributed too. Test it on a real phone, because the swap depends on a script running.

ea45d62d946b.en: <t0>Set a minimum call duration</t0>Sixty seconds is a reasonable default. Adjust once you have listened to a sample of real calls.

c858fe6aa2cd.en: <t0>Import the conversion and let it settle</t0>Do not judge the change for at least two weeks. Bidding algorithms need time, and a fortnight of local-service call data is a small sample.

18a2a56c712e.en: Call recording is a separate decision from call tracking, with separate legal obligations that vary by country and sometimes by region. Knowing that a call happened, how long it lasted and which keyword produced it is enough to optimise campaigns. Recording its contents is a bigger step, take advice before you do it.

c4fda40526ac.en: And my sample here is two businesses, in two countries, in two industries. The mechanics generalise; the numbers do not. I have not published a cost-per-call figure in this article because I do not have one I can stand behind for a named account with a stated date range, and a made-up benchmark would be worth less to you than this sentence.

b3b9c6738d35.en: Google Ads Conversion Tracking Not Working: Diagnostic Order

4ad1504eecaa.en: Google Ads showing no conversions has a short list of causes. Here they are in diagnostic order, with a check for each and why a working tag can report nothing.

1d98d31736ec.en: Google Ads reporting no conversions has a short list of causes, and they are not equally likely. Here they are in diagnostic order, with the check for each, plus the reason a working tag can still report nothing for weeks.

28de9c73e4cc.en: Why is my Google Ads conversion tracking not working?

9f0a36f692cd.en: The most frequent causes are the tag not being present on the page that confirms the action, the conversion action being set to a category or count setting that hides it, the tag firing but not being linked to the right conversion action, consent settings blocking the tag, and attribution windows meaning the conversion has not been reported yet.

efe88f384291.en: How long does Google Ads take to show conversions?

df5a3c47180f.en: Conversions can take up to 24 hours to appear in reporting, and conversions are credited to the date of the click rather than the date of the conversion. That means recent days always look worse than they eventually will, which is a normal reporting artefact rather than a fault.

6f8308fb02b8.en: How do I test if my Google Ads conversion tag is firing?

404785fa9c23.en: Use Google Tag Assistant in debug mode, complete the conversion action yourself, and confirm the conversion tag fires with the correct conversion ID and label. Then check the conversion action status in Google Ads, which should move from Unverified to Recording conversions.

1aa1f26f42fb.en: Google Ads says zero conversions. You know you got the sale.

2ac103804912.en: Google Ads reporting zero conversions usually comes down to one of five things: the <t0>tag is not on the page that confirms the action</t0>, the tag fires but is not linked to the right conversion action, the conversion action is excluded from the “Conversions” column, consent settings are blocking it, or the conversions exist but have not been reported yet because they are credited to the click date.

a9118362f0ce.en: The last one is not a fault, and it fools people constantly.

560851a9d038.en: This is one of the most-searched tracking problems there is, and the search results are dominated by forum threads where nobody arrived at an answer. That tells you something: the symptom is generic, and the cause is usually specific to how one account was wired.

7b7fd37aee61.en: So rather than listing every possibility, here is the order I actually work through, which resolves most cases in the first three steps.

00a5111d55ac.en: Before you change anything: is it actually broken?

edc535ef0fe9.en: Google Ads credits a conversion to <t0>the date of the click</t0>, not the date the conversion happened. Someone who clicked on Monday and bought on Thursday appears in Monday’s row, and until Thursday, Monday looks worse than it really was.

a26283372342.en: The practical effect is that <t0>recent days always understate performance</t0>, and they keep filling in for as long as your conversion window allows. If you are looking at the last three days and concluding tracking is broken, you may just be looking at data that has not finished arriving.

f1efeb566147.en: Look at a period that ended at least two weeks ago and is fully outside your conversion window. If that period has conversions and recent days do not, your tracking works and you were reading an incomplete report. If that older period is also zero, keep reading.

5b838be6570e.en: The conversion action status tells you where you are

5996c78aff29.en: Google Ads → <t0>Goals</t0> → <t1>Conversions</t1> → <t2>Summary</t2>. Each conversion action has a status, and it is the fastest diagnostic in the whole account.

f8390fca8ad6.en: <t0>No recent conversions</t0>: the tag was seen once but nothing lately. Usually a page or template changed.

e2189b70b11a.en: <t0>Unverified</t0>: Google has never received a signal. The tag is not firing where you think it is.

e242f6e7dd5a.en: <t0>Inactive</t0>: nothing for a long period. Treat as broken.

fe40b78ea348.en: <t0>Recording conversions</t0>: the tag is fine and your problem is elsewhere, most likely the next item.

0bff46df9ebd.en: <t0>The check</t0>Read the status before touching any code. It tells you whether this is a tagging problem or a reporting problem, and those have completely different fixes.

4bfb21414982.en: The conversion is recording but excluded from the column

cac0f62431a5.en: This one produces the maddening version of the problem: the conversion action clearly shows conversions, but your campaign view says zero. The cause is the <t0>“Include in Conversions”</t0> setting. If it is off, that action still records, it just does not appear in the Conversions column, and Smart Bidding does not bid toward it.

3bc970d73d0f.en: Secondary conversion actions are deliberately excluded by design. If someone set your main purchase action as secondary, everything looks broken while working perfectly.

3fa1f593199e.en: <t0>The check</t0>Open the conversion action and confirm the primary/secondary setting matches what you want to optimise toward.

d8510bbc1bec.en: The tag fires but carries the wrong label

f89d82347a5d.en: A Google Ads conversion tag needs both a conversion ID and a conversion <t0>label</t0>. The ID identifies the account; the label identifies which action. Copy a tag between two conversion actions and forget to change the label, and the tag fires perfectly, into the wrong bucket.

2825d8a670f4.en: <t0>The check</t0>In Tag Assistant, complete the action and read the conversion label on the fired tag. Compare it character for character with the label in the conversion action’s tag setup.

8bee5002aabb.en: Consent Mode is denying storage, and you have not modelled for it

44fe5bc47e8a.en: If you added a consent banner (and in the UK and EU you should have), tags now wait for permission. That is correct behaviour. But a banner configured to default everything to denied, with no consent update wiring, means the conversion tag never gets its permission and never fires.

f3e25335867a.en: This one has a signature: conversions drop off a cliff on the exact day the banner went live.

ce907db7e793.en: <t0>The check</t0>Load the site fresh, accept cookies, complete the action, and confirm the tag fires. Then repeat and reject, and confirm it does not. Both directions must behave as intended.

2330fbf92c97.en: The tag is not on the page that actually confirms the action

0c7a239af9d2.en: The classic. The tag is on the site but not on the thank-you page, the order-status page, or the page a customer reaches after a payment provider redirects them back. On lead-gen sites, the equivalent is a form that submits by AJAX without a page load, so a page-view-triggered tag never gets a chance to fire.

6aadc3a2ba5f.en: <t0>The check</t0>Perform the conversion yourself, then view source on the page you land on and search for the conversion ID.

09d7fb0a061e.en: Once it works, make it measure money

9fef28112782.en: Getting the tag firing is where most people stop. It is the point at which the interesting work starts, because a conversion count treats every lead as identical, and yours are not.

89a16046d3ac.en: For lead-gen accounts, <t0>enhanced conversions for leads</t0> plus offline conversion imports let you send the real value of a closed job back to Google Ads. f3b62d199a36.en: It usually means the conversion data is inflated. Common causes are duplicate pixels, purchase events firing on pages that are not orders, or duplicate events between the browser pixel and the Conversions API. 1192890dce52.en: Why does Meta show more sales than Shopify?

dfa9eba163a9.en: Some gap is normal because Meta counts view-through and click-through conversions within its attribution window, including people who did not come directly from an ad click. A large gap usually means something else: duplicate pixels, duplicate events, or a pixel firing purchase events on pages that are not real purchases.

72a42b3591f3.en: How much discrepancy between Meta and Shopify is normal?

3103ccbcb60e.en: There is no universal number, and any article quoting one is guessing. Establish your own baseline while tracking is known to be healthy, then treat deviation from your own figure as the signal rather than comparing yourself to a published average.

17458dca82d5.en: Can a second Facebook pixel cause inflated sales numbers?

0eda2d3c0fab.en: Yes. If a second pixel is installed by a third-party app and fires purchase events that do not correspond to real orders, Meta will attribute those phantom purchases to whichever campaigns are optimising toward that pixel, inflating reported sales and ROAS.

887f9d835481.en: Meta says 100 orders. Shopify says 62. Which one is lying?

2a52c1b14007.en: Some gap between Meta and Shopify is normal. Meta counts view-through conversions and uses a different attribution window than your store does. A <t0>large, persistent gap in Meta’s favour</t0> is different. It usually means something is reporting purchases that did not happen: a duplicate pixel, duplicate events, or a purchase event firing on a page that is not a purchase.

941e0c1d5c32.en: The way to tell them apart is to stop comparing totals and start comparing the right pair of numbers.

410b557a216a.en: This is one of the most common questions in ecommerce advertising, and one of the worst-served. Search it and you will find Reddit threads with thirty comments and no conclusion, Shopify Community posts marked unsolved, and vendor articles that list nine causes and then suggest their product.

2dc4f381644d.en: So here is a specific account, a specific cause, and the reconciliation that found it.

6a0959a05522.en: That gap had been running long enough that the client had stopped trusting either number. And because they could not tell which campaigns were reporting honestly, they were adjusting budgets essentially at random, increasing spend on whatever looked good in Ads Manager, with no way to know whether “good” meant anything.

982c3a76fbc7.en: That is the real damage. Not the wrong number itself, but every decision made downstream of it.

36c77898fe88.en: First: compare the correct pair of numbers

860cb1ceb54d.en: Most people compare Meta’s reported conversions against Shopify’s total orders, panic at the difference, and start rebuilding things that were never broken. Those two figures are <t0>supposed</t0> to differ.

ff559ef1a3a8.en: Every paid order, from every source

15f9cb616eaa.en: Should approach Shopify, never exceed it

1b6feda96372.en: Purchases Meta credits to your ads

43749b6efd95.en: Read the middle row again, because it is the one that matters and the one nobody looks at. <t0>Events Manager purchases should be close to your Shopify order count</t0>, since it is counting purchase events regardless of which campaign gets credit. If that number exceeds your real orders, you are not looking at an attribution question. You are looking at events that do not correspond to sales.

0190090a13d4.en: Ads Manager conversions being <t0>lower</t0> than Shopify orders is normal and healthy. Events Manager purchases being <t1>higher</t1> than Shopify orders is a defect.

dc78eadd5920.en: The account had <t0>two Meta pixels installed at the same time</t0>:

daccca90eb24.en: One installed through the official Facebook & Instagram sales channel on Shopify. This one was accurate.

ab58c8e627b4.en: One installed by a <t0>third-party app</t0>. This one was reporting purchases that never happened.

a1031043f848.en: The second pixel is the interesting one, because it was not silent. A silent pixel is easy, you notice zero conversions and go looking. This one was noisy. It reported purchases, those purchases appeared in Ads Manager, and the campaigns optimising toward it showed <t0>strong ROAS</t0>.

b71b3ffce3f1.en: None of it existed in Shopify.

81bd1e4fbf13.en: The number that made it urgent

b8880419f2aa.en: Of roughly <t0>PKR 100,000 in daily ad spend</t0>, approximately <t1>PKR 30,000 to 40,000 per day</t1> was going to campaigns optimising toward the pixel that was reporting purchases that never happened.

5d1fc7dbc6c6.en: That is <t0>30 to 40% of daily budget</t0> flowing to campaigns whose reported success was an artefact. And because those campaigns looked like the best performers in Ads Manager, they were the ones most likely to receive <t1>more</t1> budget. The reporting error was actively recruiting spend toward itself.

2f423611d96a.en: I disabled the third-party pixel. The immediate consequence was dramatic and, if you have not seen it before, alarming: <t0>every campaign optimising toward that pixel stopped delivering.</t0>

be33b62c1faf.en: That is not a side effect to be nervous about. It is the diagnosis confirming itself. Those campaigns had been running on a conversion signal that was not real; remove the signal and there is nothing left for them to optimise toward.

a461669c3644.en: The pixel loads, Pixel Helper is green, and Events Manager still shows no purchases. Seven causes in the order worth checking them, including the duplicate-pixel problem that splits your attribution in half without ever looking broken.

ddcf8d9b4680.en: Why is my Meta pixel not tracking purchases on Shopify?

cf75a17edcda.en: The most common causes are two pixels installed at once splitting the data, the pixel being absent from the page the customer actually lands on after paying, the purchase event firing without required parameters, or the checkout leaving your domain so the browser session breaks before the event can fire.

d04f1c53b14f.en: Can having two Facebook pixels cause missing purchases?

aa8b5f80f53a.en: Yes. If one pixel is installed through the Shopify sales channel and another is pasted into the theme, events can split between them. Each pixel then reports a fraction of the truth, and neither total looks obviously wrong, which is why this can run for months undetected.

d5916e6b612b.en: How do I check if my Meta pixel purchase event is working?

07e4671ee472.en: Place a real order and watch the Network tab in Chrome DevTools filtered to facebook.com or facebook.net. Confirm a Purchase event fires with value, currency and an event ID. Then confirm it arrives in Events Manager, which can take a few hours to report.

07f17d43c83c.en: Your Meta pixel fires. Your purchases still don’t show up.

12498601e6a8.en: If your Meta pixel loads but purchases never appear, check in this order: <t0>two pixels installed at once</t0>, the pixel missing from the real confirmation page, a purchase event firing without <t1>value</t1> and <t2>currency</t2>, an off-site payment redirect breaking the session, and deduplication against a Conversions API feed.

8327335e3c81.en: The first one is the most common and the hardest to spot, because nothing looks broken.

eba1b718b30d.en: “The pixel is firing” and “my purchases are tracked” are two different claims, and the gap between them is where most Shopify ad budgets leak. Pixel Helper turning green tells you a pixel exists on the page. It tells you nothing about whether the right event, with the right parameters, reached the right pixel.

6a843b589ff8.en: Start here: do you have more than one pixel?

0d95317b47b0.en: This is the first thing I check on any account, and it is the problem I have actually found in the wild rather than read about.

1f6c6280ab6b.en: On one store I audited, there were <t0>two pixels installed simultaneously</t0>, one through the Shopify integration, one pasted directly into the theme. Both were technically working. Both were reporting. Neither was reporting everything, because events were splitting between them depending on how the page loaded.

a84538b5dd23.en: The reason this survives so long is that it never looks broken. There is no error. Pixel Helper shows green. Events Manager shows purchases, just fewer than you actually had. And unless you sit down and reconcile the pixel against Shopify’s own order count, you have no reason to suspect the number is a fraction.

c500a51cd813.en: I found this on one client store, and fixing it changed what their reporting showed. I am not going to attach a percentage to the recovery, because the honest answer is that attribution splitting and budget waste are related but not identical, and I would rather give you the mechanism than a number I cannot fully defend.

5533726a030f.en: The mechanism is what matters anyway: <t0>two pixels means each one sees part of the truth</t0>, and Meta optimises on what it sees.

1ba51770c7a8.en: In Shopify admin, look in three places, because a pixel can be installed in any of them and nothing warns you about the others:

388a3f2bd10f.en: <t0>Settings → Customer events</t0>: custom pixels live here

7c7cb7c4c0a2.en: <t0>Facebook & Instagram sales channel</t0>: the official integration

b9cedae22802.en: <t0>Online Store → Themes → Edit code</t0>: search <t1>theme.liquid</t1> for <t2>fbq</t2> or <t3>connect.facebook.net</t3>

a4763c4d3d68.en: If you find a pixel ID in more than one of those, that is your problem. Pick one method, the sales channel is usually the right one, and remove the others.

b96b0e4aece5.en: The pixel is not on the page the customer actually reaches

f53cead5c41a.en: Everyone installs sitewide and assumes the confirmation page inherits it. It often does not, because that page can be rendered outside your theme. If you run post-purchase upsells, the page a customer sees immediately after paying may not be the page you think of as the thank-you page.

6a6dbc57deab.en: <t0>The check</t0>Complete a real order. On whatever page you land on, view source and search for your pixel ID. Do not infer it from the theme.

6ea1d17f8cda.en: The Purchase event fires without its required parameters

604ac333fb27.en: A <t0>Purchase</t0> event without <t1>value</t1> and <t2>currency</t2> is close to useless. Meta cannot optimise toward revenue it was never told about, and value-based bidding has nothing to work with. Missing <t3>content_ids</t3> breaks catalogue matching and dynamic retargeting on top of that.

62309301d8ed.en: <t0>The check</t0>In the Network tab, filter for <t1>facebook</t1> and read the query string on the purchase request. Confirm <t2>value</t2>, <t3>currency</t3> and <t4>content_ids</t4> are all present and populated.

c560bfa858db.en: Checkout leaves your domain and the session breaks

107bdaa98d73.en: When payment hands off to an external gateway and returns the customer to an order-received page, that round trip can break the browser session the pixel depends on. The order completes; the event does not arrive, or arrives stripped of the identifiers needed to attribute it.

94221a2cb4c6.en: <t0>The check</t0>Does your payment flow leave your domain? If so, browser-only tracking is best-effort and you need the Conversions API.

6e857c1aadfd.en: Deduplication is removing the event on purpose

38d82505b5ff.en: If you run the pixel and the Conversions API together (which you should), Meta deduplicates using <t0>event_id</t0>. When the browser and server disagree about what that ID is, you either double-count everything or silently lose one side. Losing one side looks exactly like “the pixel stopped working.”

e34596fad05b.en: <t0>The check</t0>For one order, capture the <t1>event_id</t1> the browser sent and the one your server sent. They must be identical.

9db2e7bfc89f.en: A meaningful share of traffic blocks browser-based tracking outright. This is not a bug you can fix, it is a permanent tax on client-side measurement, and it is the reason a browser-only setup will always undercount. The fix is not a fix; it is the Conversions API.

0f7023a447fa.en: <t0>The check</t0>Compare Events Manager purchase counts with Shopify’s order count for the same period. A persistent gap that scales with volume is usually this.

b37441ebd4bf.en: Events Manager reporting is not instant. Before concluding an event is missing, wait a few hours and look again. I have watched people rewrite a working checkout because they checked a dashboard ninety seconds after a test order.

da32602a9e67.en: <t0>The check</t0>Use the Test Events tool for immediate feedback; use Events Manager for volume, tomorrow.

feff648d7696.en: Here is the exercise that finds problems no checklist will. Pick one week. Write down three numbers:

cb879bf987f9.en: A subset, not all sales come from ads

8f6ac98bb772.en: Most people compare the wrong pair and panic. Ads Manager conversions <t0>should</t0> be lower than Shopify orders, because not every customer came from an ad. The number that should be close to Shopify is <t1>Events Manager purchases</t1>. If that one is far below your order count, you have a tracking problem rather than an attribution question.

fd32dd765553.en: And if Events Manager is <t0>higher</t0> than Shopify, you have the opposite problem, usually duplicate events, which is <t1>a different article</t1>.

80753a73304b.en: What I am not telling you

5b900e400b11.en: I have not given you an expected discrepancy percentage, because the honest range depends on your traffic mix, your checkout, your customers’ browsers and your country, and every published benchmark I have seen comes from a company selling the fix. Establish your own baseline when things are working, and treat deviation from <t0>your</t0> number as the signal.

3cca71fd3d6e.en: The ranking above reflects a small number of accounts plus what the failure modes logically imply. Treat it as a sensible search order rather than a statistic.

f6f3c200049c.en: Want someone to just look at it?

54abf50dfdcf.en: Send me your store URL. I will tell you what your pixel is actually doing, and you do not need to give me access to anything to start.

1b4a84374b60.en: Is Your Meta Pixel Reporting Purchases That Never Happened?

02f24b327bc0.en: A pixel that stops reporting is obvious. The costly failure is one that reports too much, because inflated ROAS attracts budget. Six ways to check yours.

24ebe1e9eeeb.en: Can a Facebook pixel report purchases that did not happen?

babcfc871da5.en: Yes. A misconfigured pixel can fire a purchase event on a page that is not a completed order, fire repeatedly on page refreshes, or be installed by a third-party app that triggers events on the wrong conditions. Meta records what it receives, so those events appear as real purchases in reporting.

ec0119c874de.en: How do I know if my Meta pixel data is accurate?

aae7393b63c2.en: Reconcile a settled week. Compare Events Manager purchase count against your store order count for the same period and timezone. Events Manager should approach your order count and never exceed it. If it exceeds it, you have phantom or duplicate events.

5418e786d870.en: Why does my Facebook ROAS look good but I have no sales?

91d8d8f26649.en: Because ROAS is calculated from the conversion data the pixel reports, not from your bank account. If the pixel is reporting purchases that never happened, ROAS is computed on revenue that does not exist and will look excellent while the business makes nothing.

959ef04016e2.en: A silent pixel is easy. A lying pixel takes your budget with it.

98323b3697fb.en: A pixel that stops reporting gets noticed within days, because conversions fall to zero and someone panics. A pixel that reports <t0>too much</t0> can run for months, because inflated ROAS looks like success, and Meta responds by sending more budget toward the campaigns producing it.

d34f7f2af0bf.en: The only reliable test is reconciliation: does the purchase count in Events Manager correspond to real orders in your store?

cdd95180a73e.en: Almost every troubleshooting article treats missing conversions as the problem. In practice the more damaging failure runs the other way, because it does not look like a failure. It looks like your best campaign.

59c6f37697b7.en: Why over-reporting is worse than under-reporting

2bdf352636c4.en: Under-reporting costs you optimisation quality. Meta sees fewer conversions than really happened, so it learns more slowly and you probably under-invest in something that works. Bad, but self-limiting.

c281db6edd40.en: Over-reporting is different, because it creates a feedback loop. Inflated conversions produce inflated ROAS. Inflated ROAS makes a campaign look like a winner. Winners get more budget. More budget produces more phantom conversions.

9b1175b8c852.en: <t0>The error recruits spend toward itself.</t0> That is why it can consume a third of a daily budget before anyone questions it, every signal available inside Ads Manager says the campaign is working.

4825c0f34e1f.en: The single highest-value check, and most accounts have never had it done. Take one week that ended at least two weeks ago. Compare Events Manager purchases against your store’s order count for the same period and timezone.

41e6d75dafbe.en: Events Manager should approach your order count. It should never exceed it. Events Manager counts purchase events, and a purchase event without an order is by definition not a purchase.

155676215d4b.en: <t0>Verdict</t0>Events Manager higher than store orders means phantom or duplicate events. Nothing about attribution windows explains this away.

c124276cd789.en: On the account behind this article, the cause was a second pixel installed by a third-party app, reporting purchases with no corresponding orders. Check <t0>Settings → Customer events</t0>, the <t1>Facebook & Instagram sales channel</t1>, and <t2>theme.liquid</t2>. More than one pixel ID is your first suspect, see <t3>the article on multiple pixels</t3>.

0699af8ab602.en: <t0>Verdict</t0>Two pixel IDs and a discrepancy in the same account is rarely a coincidence.

99cb783598b2.en: Check whether the purchase event fires on a refresh

24565c2497aa.en: Complete a real order, land on the confirmation page, then refresh it. Watch the Network tab. If a second purchase event fires, every customer who refreshes, bookmarks or revisits that page is inflating your numbers. Without a unique <t0>event_id</t0> or order identifier, Meta has no way to know it is the same sale.

2d52b877ae14.en: <t0>Verdict</t0>A purchase event on refresh means your counts drift upward with traffic, not with sales.

ea7aa83ec533.en: Check what page the purchase event is bound to

7c1e5dca21fa.en: A purchase event should fire on order completion and nowhere else. Misconfigured apps sometimes bind it to add-to-cart, initiate-checkout, or any page matching a loose URL rule. Every one of those produces purchases with no orders behind them.

7e6747f10eec.en: <t0>Verdict</t0>Walk your funnel with the Network tab open. A purchase event before payment is a defect, not an optimisation.

f29fc4e8a8ae.en: Segment reported conversions by campaign, then trace them

763295ef18d3.en: Do not evaluate the account as one number. Group campaigns by which pixel they optimise toward, then try to trace each group’s claimed orders in your store. On that account, one group’s orders could not be traced at all, and that group was consuming roughly 30 to 40% of daily spend.

fa362705680c.en: <t0>Verdict</t0>A campaign group whose orders you cannot find in your store is the leak.

a5e008ef5d5f.en: Compare purchase value against real revenue

e12f73b47105.en: Counts can look plausible while values are nonsense. Compare total purchase value reported for a settled week against actual revenue for the same week. A value materially above real revenue means events are firing with wrong or duplicated values, even if the count looks close.

573a1584af39.en: <t0>Verdict</t0>Check both count and value. They fail independently.

ea66f9f56b09.en: What to do when you find it

fa4028f451fd.en: Fix the source rather than the symptom. Disabling a misconfigured pixel or correcting the event trigger will cause the affected campaigns to stop delivering, that is the diagnosis confirming itself, not a new problem.

91b815869b96.en: Then brief whoever owns the budget <t0>before</t0> they see the dashboard. Reported ROAS will fall. Revenue will not, because the revenue you are removing never existed. That conversation is much easier held in advance than in retrospect.

e7d9220453b3.en: If a campaign has been optimising toward phantom conversions for months, Meta has spent that time learning to find people who trigger phantom conversions. Rebuilding on clean data takes time, and early performance on the corrected setup will look worse than the fiction it replaced. That is the cost of having been wrong, not the cost of fixing it.

206e4c5a70b8.en: One account, one cause. Over-reporting has other sources, duplicate CAPI events without matching identifiers, test events left running, several apps firing the same conversion. The reconciliation in check one detects all of them; identifying which requires the rest.

faf55d9f0f03.en: I am also not giving you a threshold for “too much”. Compare against your own store’s orders. That comparison is exact, which is more than any benchmark can offer.

6710b6abe3a9.en: It takes fifteen minutes to find out and most accounts have never been checked. Send me your store URL.

125d680d8f9e.en: Scaling advice says double down on your best ROAS. That assumes reported ROAS reflects real sales. When it does not, scaling accelerates the loss.

2d1810d851a4.en: How do I know which Facebook campaign to scale?

9dc4b33adff8.en: Scale the campaign whose reported orders you can trace in your store. Before comparing ROAS between campaigns, reconcile reported purchases against real orders, because a campaign with inflated conversion data will always appear to be your best performer.

4584e7deb1e6.en: Why did my ROAS drop after scaling?

98dd0fad277f.en: Common causes include audience saturation, moving out of the algorithm learning phase, and increased competition. But if the drop was immediate and severe, check whether the pre-scaling ROAS was real, because inflated conversion data produces excellent apparent performance that cannot survive contact with a larger budget.

6836e5a14a4b.en: Should I scale a campaign with high ROAS but no matching revenue?

1605c7ee7b30.en: No. A campaign reporting strong ROAS while your store shows no corresponding orders is reporting conversions that did not happen. Scaling it increases spend against a signal that does not exist.

fa8c69b5ae6d.en: Every scaling guide assumes your numbers are real. Check that first.

4d1bb4407d45.en: Every scaling guide says the same thing: find your best ROAS and put more money behind it. That is reasonable advice resting on an assumption almost nobody tests: <t0>that reported ROAS reflects sales that actually happened.</t0>

d651b8093fcf.en: When it does not, scaling does not amplify a winner. It amplifies a reporting error, and it does so faster than you will notice.

7d64d1763026.en: There is no shortage of scaling content. Increase budgets by 20% every three days. Duplicate into new audiences. Vertical versus horizontal scaling. Most of it is fine as far as it goes.

0f139e826e0a.en: What almost none of it includes is a step zero: <t0>verify the performance you are about to scale is real.</t0> That omission is how a client I worked with ended up putting more budget behind their worst campaigns for months.

1c1966323999.en: Scaling rules select for the highest reported ROAS. A campaign optimising toward a pixel that over-reports will always show a higher ROAS than one measuring honestly, not because it performs better, but because its denominator is fiction.

cf0e760d840d.en: So the selection rule that is supposed to find your best campaign reliably finds your <t0>most inaccurately measured</t0> one. And every scaling cycle sends more budget to it.

2693bb797b43.en: What that looked like in practice

969f49792bef.en: The client was running roughly PKR 100,000 a day across the account, and adjusting budgets essentially at random, because they could not tell which campaigns were reporting honestly, they were increasing and decreasing spend based on a dashboard nobody trusted. Their words for it were that they were making changes blindly.

004618a0f610.en: The account had two pixels. One accurate, one reporting purchases with no corresponding orders. Meta showed around 100 orders; the store had 55 to 70. Roughly <t0>30 to 40% of daily budget</t0> was in campaigns attached to the inaccurate pixel, and those campaigns showed the strongest ROAS in the account.

420be8bdce70.en: Under any standard scaling rule, those were the campaigns to scale. That is the part worth sitting with. <t0>The methodology was not being applied badly. It was being applied correctly to bad data</t0>, which produced exactly the wrong answer with total confidence.

8605d2b16e39.en: Step zero, before any scaling decision

472076ab3fbf.en: <t0>Reconcile one settled week</t0>Events Manager purchases against real store orders. If Events Manager is higher, stop, you have phantom or duplicate events and no campaign comparison is valid yet.

aa5afcb90740.en: <t0>Trace the specific campaign you intend to scale</t0>Not the account. That campaign. Can you find its claimed orders in your store? If you cannot trace them, do not scale it.

f4deb8e4b3a0.en: <t0>Check which pixel it optimises toward</t0>If the account has more than one pixel, campaigns are not comparable until you know which is which.

b775181b1ace.en: <t0>Then apply whatever scaling method you like</t0>The methods are fine. They just needed something true to operate on.

3fa5d2a3270e.en: If you have ever scaled a campaign with excellent ROAS and watched performance collapse immediately, not decay over a fortnight, but collapse, consider that the original figure may not have been real. Genuine winners degrade gradually as audiences saturate. Fictional ones do not degrade at all, because there was nothing there to degrade; the reported number simply stops looking plausible next to your bank balance.

acc3d9e21b22.en: Reported ROAS is a proxy for the thing you actually care about, which is money arriving in the business. The closer your optimisation signal sits to real revenue, the harder it is to fool:

fc73d790b051.en: Hard, an order either exists or it does not

d7eee072c2f5.en: Hardest, and the one that pays wages

f2544c31761a.en: Best, if you can measure it

590724a109b0.en: Most advertisers never move past the first row. Moving to the second, simply confirming the orders exist, costs an hour a week and removes the entire class of problem this article describes.

bb8420536749.en: None of this makes scaling easy. Audience saturation, creative fatigue, learning-phase resets and competition are all real, and they will still cost you performance on a campaign whose data is perfect.

9e13051d20af.en: The narrow claim here is that those problems are worth solving <t0>after</t0> you have confirmed the number you are optimising toward corresponds to sales. One account is not a study, but the mechanism is not exotic, and the check is cheap enough that there is no good reason to skip it.

1a444586f1b3.en: Make sure the performance you are scaling is real. Send me your store URL and I will reconcile it against your store.

a0f9d7d07533.en: Shopify's 26 August Deadline: Did Your Tracking Survive?

2fe3aaf8ba6e.en: Shopify's 26 August 2026 upgrade removes Additional Scripts from Thank you pages. See which purchase tags it affects and check yours in ten minutes.

f7d101b08d97.en: What was scheduled to happen on 26 August 2026 for Shopify stores?

356a5f5bf53e.en: Non-Plus Shopify stores that have not manually upgraded their Thank you and Order status pages are upgraded automatically. Customisations built with Additional Scripts and deprecated script tags on those two pages are removed rather than migrated.

b986a3b45806.en: Does the Shopify checkout upgrade remove my Facebook pixel?

b7d3de2f5719.en: It removes any pixel or tag installed through Additional Scripts on the Thank you and Order status pages. A Meta pixel connected through the official Facebook & Instagram sales channel is not affected. The risk is specifically hand-pasted code.

788c05d25ced.en: How do I check what is in my Shopify Additional Scripts box?

0819e1279b61.en: Go to Settings, then Checkout, and look at the Additional scripts field. Since 28 August 2025 it is view-only, but you can still read what is in it. Anything there that fires a conversion was due to be replaced before 26 August 2026, so check whether yours was.

5f9788f7fed0.en: Shopify’s 26 August deadline has passed. Did your purchase tracking survive?

3266db95f51b.en: The 26 August 2026 deadline has now passed. I wrote this on 12 August as a warning, and I have not verified what happened on individual stores since. If your reported purchases dropped after 26 August, compare your ad platforms against your Shopify orders for the days before and after, then work through the check below.

15fe15a22ab6.en: On <t0>26 August 2026</t0>, Shopify scheduled an automatic upgrade for every non-Plus store that had not already migrated its Thank you and Order status pages. Anything running through <t1>Additional Scripts</t1> on those pages, Google Ads conversion tags, Meta pixel purchase events, GTM containers, affiliate scripts, is, according to Shopify’s documentation, <t2>removed, not migrated</t2>.

5e8b8a41dee3.en: If you did nothing, your purchase tracking should have stopped on that date while your ad platforms kept spending as though nothing had happened.

c6ba252a64d5.en: This was the rare tracking problem with a date on it. Most of what I write about is a slow leak you can fix whenever you notice. This one arrived for a large population of stores simultaneously, and the stores affected are precisely the ones least likely to be watching, because the change happens <t0>to</t0> them, not because of anything they did.

d3f3b64e5597.en: “August 26, 2026 is the deadline for stores on a non-Plus Shopify subscription plan to upgrade their existing Thank you and Order status pages to the new version of those pages.”

939b8b6886c6.en: Stores that do not upgrade manually are upgraded automatically. Shopify Plus stores passed this milestone on 28 August 2025.

accf73657544.en: The word doing the damage is <t0>removed</t0>. Not migrated, not converted, not preserved in a compatibility layer. Shopify replaces the old Thank you and Order status pages with new ones, and customisations that depended on the old rendering model do not come along.

97d1e3851e45.en: Google Ads conversion tag pasted into Additional Scripts

c7dca664e4be.en: Custom Pixel, or Google & YouTube channel

dd385fc96377.en: Meta pixel Purchase event in Additional Scripts

919421223704.en: Custom Pixel, or Facebook & Instagram channel

4ea2f6a69740.en: GTM container loaded on the thank-you page

22414c2ad94a.en: Meta pixel via the official sales channel

06a0a5d2b24c.en: Google tag via the Google & YouTube channel

0a3414f2d785.en: Unaffected, it never depended on the page

2ec0296fde85.en: Read the last row twice. <t0>Server-side tracking is the only row that was never at risk</t0>, because it does not depend on a browser rendering a page Shopify controls. That is the real lesson of this deadline, and it will still be true the next time a platform changes something underneath you.

a97a83df6ab6.en: <t0>Read your Additional Scripts box</t0>Shopify admin → <t1>Settings</t1> → <t2>Checkout</t2> → <t3>Additional scripts</t3>. It has been view-only since 28 August 2025, but you can still read it. Copy the contents somewhere safe.

e19eb28bfc9d.en: <t0>Find anything that fires a conversion</t0>Search that text for <t1>gtag</t1>, <t2>fbq</t2>, <t3>googletagmanager</t3>, <t4>snaptr</t4>, <t5>ttq</t5>, or any <t6><script src=</t6>. Every hit is a tag that was due to stop working on 26 August.

81ca81146689.en: <t0>Check what your platforms think they are receiving</t0>Open Google Ads → Goals → Conversions, and Meta Events Manager. Compare daily purchase volume for the days before and after 26 August. That before-and-after comparison is your proof, without it you cannot show that anything broke, or that you fixed it.

ea5eb633c2cd.en: <t0>Rebuild each one as a Custom Pixel</t0>Shopify admin → <t1>Settings</t1> → <t2>Customer events</t2> → <t3>Add custom pixel</t3>. Custom Pixels run in a sandbox and subscribe to events such as <t4>checkout_completed</t4>.

fc3c1aa5f3e5.en: <t0>Verify with a real order</t0>Not a test link. A real purchase, on a phone, through the actual checkout. Then confirm the event arrived in the platform, not just that it fired in the browser.

bb794aba55e5.en: Migrating to a Custom Pixel is the right move, and it introduces a failure mode most guides skip.

0eee6e474f78.en: <t0>checkout_completed</t0> is <t1>not guaranteed to fire on the thank-you page</t1>. With post-purchase upsells enabled it can fire on the first upsell page instead, and if that page fails to load, it may not fire at all. Practitioners have also reported a race condition where the pixel fires before customer data is populated, producing events with near-zero match quality.

87e4a2bf56b0.en: I have seen both behaviours described by multiple independent practitioners, but I have not reproduced them on a store I control. Treat them as things to test for rather than facts to repeat. If you run post-purchase upsells, test that path specifically, it is the one most likely to bite.

30b7b528558b.en: What it looks like when it hits

b8121ccaf4ab.en: Nothing dramatic. That is the problem.

0c4b9014140d.en: Your ads keep running. Your budget keeps spending. Orders keep arriving in Shopify. The only thing that changes is that Google Ads and Meta stop being told which clicks produced those orders, so Smart Bidding, which optimises toward conversions it can see, starts optimising toward a signal that has quietly gone to zero.

cf37f0358991.en: You will notice it as a sudden drop in reported conversions and a rise in cost per acquisition, roughly a week later, with no obvious cause. By then the algorithm has been learning from bad data for seven days.

628249c0569d.en: The 26 August date and the auto-upgrade behaviour come from Shopify’s own help documentation, verified on 12 August 2026, before the deadline. fae6fd92088d.en: So do not take the table as permission to skip step one. Read your own Additional Scripts box. What is in there is the only list that matters.

2c7d39c55c56.en: Where a Snapchat purchase event dies

b513d9691eec.en: The customer journey from ad click to Snapchat Events Manager, with the six failure causes marked beneath the stage where each one occurs: pixel re-initialisation at checkout, session loss at the payment gateway, lowercase event name, missing transaction ID and missing pixel at the confirmation page, and deduplication at Snapchat.

5d35707e11b7.en: <t0>The confirmation page is where most of it goes wrong.</t0> Three of the six causes bite at the final step, which is also the step people test least, because testing it properly means spending real money.

0b6574696734.en: Snapchat tracking gets far less written about than Meta or Google, which means when it breaks you are mostly on your own. The articles that do exist tend to be written by companies selling a tracking product, so they stop at "install our app." This is the sequence I actually run, in the order I run it, and why that order.

2733fdceae9d.en: First: confirm the event genuinely isn't arriving

986c8e2a8c70.en: Before changing anything, establish whether the event is missing or merely delayed. Two checks, sixty seconds.

f3d597142501.en: <t0>Check the network, not the dashboard.</t0> Open your confirmation page in Chrome, open DevTools (F12), go to the <t1>Network</t1> tab, and filter for <t2>tr.snapchat.com</t2>. Complete a real test purchase. If you see a request fire with your pixel ID and the event name, the browser is doing its job and your problem is downstream, reporting, deduplication, or attribution. If nothing fires, the problem is on the page.

1ca57eeee5f6.en: The <t0>Snap Pixel Helper</t0> browser extension does the same job with a friendlier interface, and will also tell you whether the pixel is installed at all. I use the Network tab because it shows the exact payload, and the payload is usually where the answer is.

a6e97bc48637.en: What a healthy Snapchat event sequence looks like in the Network tab

19accfec5674.en: A DevTools network panel filtered to tr.snapchat.com, showing four requests in order: PAGE_VIEW, VIEW_CONTENT, ADD_CART and PURCHASE, each returning status 200. The PURCHASE row is highlighted as the one that must be present and must carry a transaction ID.

b91c581936b0.en: <t0>If the first three appear and the fourth doesn't, your problem is on the confirmation page.</t0> If none of them appear, the pixel isn't installed where you think it is.

41a83578f9c5.en: Events Manager reporting is not instant. Before concluding an event is missing, wait a few hours and re-check. I have watched people rewrite a working checkout because they looked at a dashboard ninety seconds after a test order.

09e7d6a38fae.en: Snapchat's standard events are <t0>uppercase</t0>: <t1>PURCHASE</t1>, <t2>ADD_CART</t2>, <t3>PAGE_VIEW</t3>, <t4>START_CHECKOUT</t4>. If you send <t5>purchase</t5>, it is not recognised as a standard event. The insidious part is that it may still fire and still appear somewhere, it simply won't be treated as the standard conversion, so campaign optimisation and reporting behave as though nothing happened.

880f857d94cf.en: This is number one because it produces the exact symptom people describe, "the pixel is firing but Events Manager shows nothing", and because copying a Meta implementation across is a natural thing to do. Meta uses <t0>Purchase</t0>. Snapchat does not.

8ad078f8887a.en: <t0>The check</t0>In the Network tab, read the event name in the request payload. It must be exactly <t1>PURCHASE</t1>. Capitalisation is not cosmetic here.

1f14ff2e8879.en: Without <t0>transaction_id</t0>, Snapchat has no way to tell a genuine second order from the same customer refreshing the confirmation page. Snap documents a <t1>30-day deduplication window</t1> on <t2>transaction_id</t2>, versus 48 hours for <t3>client_dedup_id</t3>.

7ff55ea61691.en: The failure mode cuts both ways, which is why it belongs this high. Omit it and refreshes inflate your purchase count. Send a value that isn't actually unique per order (a cart ID, a checkout ID, a session ID) and legitimate orders get collapsed into one and <t0>vanish</t0>. The second case looks exactly like "my events aren't firing."

c579f3077958.en: <t0>The check</t0>Place two test orders. Confirm the <t1>transaction_id</t1> differs between them, and that it matches the order number your store actually assigns.

99cbb76d38fc.en: The pixel isn't on the page that actually confirms the order

c1fab7351ec9.en: Almost everyone installs the pixel sitewide and assumes the confirmation page inherits it. Frequently it doesn't. Hosted checkouts, order-status pages and post-purchase upsell flows are often rendered outside the theme or template that carries your tracking code.

935b2a891da2.en: Worth checking specifically: if you run a post-purchase upsell, the page a customer lands on immediately after paying may not be the page you think of as the thank-you page.

e52eaa950fbc.en: <t0>The check</t0>Complete a real order. On the page you land on, view source and search for your pixel ID. Do not infer it from the theme, look at the page the customer is actually on.

610c48da2c3f.en: An off-site payment redirect breaks the session

c17ee5aa278d.en: When checkout hands off to an external gateway and returns the customer to an order-received page, that round trip can break the browser session the pixel depends on. The purchase completes, the customer sees their confirmation, and the event never reaches Snapchat, or arrives stripped of the identifiers needed to attribute it.

c0f4f885648a.en: This is the point where a browser-only setup stops being sufficient. Server-side tracking via the <t0>Conversions API</t0> is the durable fix, because the event originates from your server and never depends on surviving a redirect.

56f01aa62280.en: <t0>The check</t0>Does your payment flow leave your domain? If yes, treat browser-only tracking as best-effort and plan for CAPI.

fccb8b52b8e8.en: A single-page checkout re-initialises the pixel

c56e4c9dae9b.en: In single-page applications, if pixel initialisation runs on every virtual page view, the pixel's state resets each time. Advanced matching data gathered earlier in the flow is lost, so the purchase event arrives without the identifiers that make it useful, thin, poorly matched, and sometimes unattributed.

e669f59fa11d.en: The event fires. It just doesn't carry what it needs, which is why this one is easy to misread as "working."

a1a8a7314be5.en: <t0>The check</t0>Watch the Network tab through the whole checkout. Initialisation should happen once. Events should fire many times.

a9746c5728a8.en: If you run the pixel <t0>and</t0> the Conversions API (which you should), Snapchat deduplicates using <t1>client_dedup_id</t1> (48-hour window) or <t2>transaction_id</t2> (30 days). Two events sharing an identifier are counted once, by design.

9b5f98aa9e48.en: It becomes a problem when the browser and server sides disagree about what that identifier is. Get the mapping wrong and you either double-count everything or silently lose one side. Snap's guidance is that non-purchase events map to <t0>client_dedup_id</t0>, and purchase events map to <t1>transaction_id</t1>, and crucially, <t2>the value must match across every path sending that event</t2>.

b8fb14c7c4f1.en: Horizontal bar chart on a shared 30-day axis. transaction_id deduplicates over 30 days. client_dedup_id deduplicates over 48 hours, which is about one fifteenth of that span.

8ae6516403da.en: <t0>Why the identifier you choose matters.</t0> A purchase deduplicated on <t1>transaction_id</t1> stays protected for 30 days. On <t2>client_dedup_id</t2> that protection expires after 48 hours, which is why Snap maps purchases to <t3>transaction_id</t3> and everything else to <t4>client_dedup_id</t4>.

796f8874c82b.en: <t0>The check</t0>For one order, capture the identifier the browser sent and the identifier your server sent. They must be identical. Not similar: identical.

d5ba528c67b8.en: Where my own numbers come from

a15bf95227d5.en: I don't have a large client sample on Snapchat, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I have is one store I ran end to end, my own, where the tracking worked, which is the only reason I can talk about what a healthy Snapchat setup produces.

14ec07f666d0.en: AlphaMart: my own store, not a client

b9f3e16444a1.en: Context that matters, because otherwise these figures flatter me: at 5.69× on $1,452 that's roughly $8,262 in tracked revenue across 1,034 orders, an average order value of about $8. This was a low-ticket product. A $1.40 cost per purchase is a very different achievement at $8 AOV than it would be at $80, and anyone quoting a CPA without an AOV beside it is showing you half a number.

9b0affdc1997.en: The figures are from a period ending May 2024. I'm dating them rather than presenting them as current.

1c00a24c3ef7.en: Snapchat Ads Manager for Alpha Mart showing US$1,452.18 spent, 11,076,872 paid impressions, 242,131 clicks, 2.19% click rate, 1,034 purchases and US$1.40 cost per purchase, over 4 November 2023 to 7 May 2024.

295ef98d49b1.en: <t0>What this screenshot does and doesn't prove.</t0> It corroborates the spend (US$1,452.18), the purchase count (1,034), the cost per purchase (US$1.40) and the date range. It also shows 11,076,872 impressions and 242,131 clicks at a 2.19% click rate. It does <t1>not</t1> show ROAS, that figure comes from store-side revenue, not from this view, and you should treat any number you can't see in the frame accordingly.

9ae29a7a2f97.en: The reason 1,034 purchases matter for this article isn't the ROAS. It's that a store sending a clean, correctly-named, properly-deduplicated <t0>PURCHASE</t0> event at that volume gives you a reliable baseline for what "working" looks like, and makes it obvious when something has stopped.

4f9a34be4920.en: Two honest limitations, because an article that admits none is usually hiding some.

dd8db2799fc9.en: <t0>I can't give you a frequency ranking from a large sample.</t0> The order above reflects a small number of accounts plus what the failure modes logically imply, a lowercase event name breaks reporting deterministically, so it belongs at the top regardless of how often I have personally seen it. Treat the ranking as a sensible search order, not a statistic.

dd7e0b25f835.en: <t0>Snapchat's interface changes.</t0> Menu paths go stale quickly, which is why the checks above are anchored to the network request and the payload rather than to where a button currently sits. The payload is the thing that's actually true.

f6a6aa699d31.en: Open the Network tab, filter <t0>tr.snapchat.com</t0>, place a test order.

c9618c8ccfc3.en: Confirm the event name is exactly <t0>PURCHASE</t0>, uppercase.

3f0d93e7ee07.en: Confirm <t0>transaction_id</t0> is present and unique per order.

d43cbf279420.en: Confirm the pixel exists on the page the customer actually lands on.

428be7200ba6.en: If checkout leaves your domain, plan for the Conversions API.

11befb10b462.en: If you run pixel and CAPI, confirm the dedup identifier matches exactly on both sides.

9e457d711495.en: If you get through all six and the event still doesn't arrive, the problem is usually not the pixel, it's that the page you're testing isn't the page your customers reach. Go back and complete a real purchase with real money, on a phone, from an ad click. Test orders through a staging link skip precisely the parts that break.
